title: Liquidity and Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift (Sadka 2006; Chordia, Goyal, Sadka, Sadka & Shivakumar 2009)
one_line: PEAD lives almost entirely in illiquid stocks — long-short PEAD earns 0.04%/month in the most liquid stocks vs 2.43% in the most illiquid (Chordia et al. 2009), and trading costs eat 70-100% of the paper profits; Sadka (2006) finds momentum and PEAD returns partly compensate for systematic liquidity (informed-trading) risk.

findings.statement: PEAD concentrated in highly illiquid stocks: value-weighted long-short 0.04%/month (most liquid) vs 2.43%/month (most illiquid).
findings.evidence: Chordia et al., Financial Analysts Journal 65(4), 2009.

findings.statement: Transaction costs account for 70-100% of the paper profits.
Unexpected market-wide changes in the variable (informed-trading) component of price impact are priced in momentum and PEAD portfolio returns.
findings.evidence: Sadka, Journal of Financial Economics 80(2), 2006; intraday data 1983-2001.

why.pattern: Limits to arbitrage / liquidity risk: the drift survives where it is too costly to trade and partly pays for bearing liquidity risk.

reported_results.headline: Liquid stocks 0.04%/month vs illiquid 2.43%/month; costs eat 70-100%.

tradable_edge: Stock-level; confirms PEAD is not tradable in liquid names after costs — keep the PEAD stock specs parked.

decay_risk.reason: PEAD gone for large stocks since 2006 (Martineau 2021).

data_fit: Single-stock study — not testable on our ES/NQ data.
caveats: Abstract-level for both papers (full texts paywalled).
